Musk Is Willing To Crash Tesla Into the Ground so That SpaceX Could Pick Up the Pieces at a Bargain
8 photos
Photo: Tesla
Elon Musk hasn't made a secret of the fact that he wants to fold Tesla into SpaceX. After Musk said committees have been meeting to discuss merger plans, things appear to have advanced to the point that an official announcement is imminent. According to a new report, Elon Musk's two companies will sign the biggest-ever deal as soon as December.
Everyone who has followed Tesla since the early days knows that it's no ordinary company, and Elon Musk is no ordinary CEO. However, the past two years have been a rollercoaster ride. Starting in 2023, Musk has changed Tesla's course, with visible effects into 2024.
At first, it was the cancellation of the Mexico gigafactory, supposedly to speed up the development of Tesla's next-generation EVs and the unboxed manufacturing process. Then, in 2024, Musk appeared to have lost his mind, firing entire teams to cull the workforce in preparation for a market crash that is yet to come. Then he went full MAGA in 2025, jeopardizing Tesla's fate for a future that has now been proven a mistake.
Musk hates that he lost control of Tesla The start of 2026 opened a new window into Musk's vision, or lack thereof. In January, during the Q4 2025 earnings call, Tesla's CEO announced the demise of the Model S/X program, while also revealing that Tesla invested $2 billion in xAI, despite a shareholder vote rejecting the proposal. Musk also announced a $20 billion investment plan, with none of this money going to the automotive sector.
It was the first sign that the controversial CEO had indeed given up on Tesla being a carmaker. Instead, the investments were earmarked for developing new projects in robotics and AI, including data centers. Soon after that, reports indicated that Musk was seriously considering the idea of merging his companies under one big umbrella that he controls.
Not later than February, SpaceX already swallowed the money-losing xAI. If you don't remember, Musk funded xAI as a side project and began diverting resources from Tesla, including GPUs destined for Tesla's data centers. He also used xAI to buy Twitter, thus moving the loss from one company to another. Well, SpaceX investors don't seem to mind, considering that I've heard no complaints about paying for xAI.
Photo: Tesla However, Musk has his eyes on a much bigger prize: he wants Tesla, no less. xAI may have been a diversion to solve some immediate problem, but Tesla was the crown jewel. The truth is, Musk absolutely hates that he no longer has enough Tesla shares to control the company. He sold many of his Tesla shares to buy Twitter as a way to control the narrative prior to the 2024 elections.
A Tesla-SpaceX merger effectively brings Tesla under Musk's control That's why Musk fought tooth and nail for a massive compensation package, even taking Tesla out of Delaware and incorporating it into Texas to secure the bonus. Musk was afraid that his diminished stake in Tesla would make him easy to remove from the company. Indeed, Musk controls about 20% of Tesla, and prospects of gaining more shares are entirely tied to the compensation packages that are yet to come into effect.
However, Musk controls about 85% of SpaceX, and he's not willing to make the same mistake he made with Tesla to dilute his stake. He doesn't want less control; he wants more. That's the idea behind this mega-merger between SpaceX and Tesla. Basically, Musk wants SpaceX, which he controls, to incorporate Tesla, which he doesn't. When the two entities merge, Musk effectively becomes the ruler of Tesla, or whatever remains of it.
Even though Musk never put it that way, it was clear from February that he was essentially preparing a hostile takeover of Tesla by his (then) private company SpaceX. Everything he's done since then appears to converge toward achieving this goal. And it was obvious from the beginning that the less Tesla is valued, the more control Musk has over it after a merger with SpaceX.
For the best merger, Tesla must lose, and SpaceX must gain value Musk has already prepared for this step by increasing the valuation of the money-losing xAI in preparation for the merger with SpaceX. As a result, the February merger artificially increased SpaceX's valuation. Given the outsized stake that Musk owned in both SpaceX and xAI, the merger also strengthened Musk's position before taking over Tesla.
Photo: Tesla That's half the work, though, and the other half is undermining Tesla's position and causing its shares to drop. An undervalued Tesla is a boon for SpaceX and, indeed, Musk, when the SpaceX-Tesla merger completes. And, again, Musk appears to deliver on this front by undermining Tesla's automotive business.
After scrapping the Model S and Model X, the Cybertruck was a natural victim. Officially, all of them had to go because they sold poorly and Tesla had bigger projects to devote to. The Optimus robot line was supposed to replace the Model S/X production line, while the Cybertruck was killed to make way for more Cybercabs. Except neither Optimus nor the Cybercab requires more production capacity. The former doesn't exist, and the latter is already littering parking lots because there's not much use for it.
The most egregious part is not that the slow-selling vehicles have been discontinued, but that Tesla has no plans to build new car models. The Cybertruck platform could've been used for a three-row SUV that everyone wanted. However, Musk has different plans, and a successful Tesla would've interfered with them.
A Tesla-SpaceX merger is no longer hypothetical; it's official Back in January, Bloomberg reported that Musk had already set up two entities in Nevada with the phrase "merger sub" in their names. Both list SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen as an officer, confirming that SpaceX would get an outsized role in this merger. During the SpaceX third-quarter earnings call in October, Musk confirmed that special committees from Tesla and SpaceX are already at work to draw up a merger plan.
Photo: Tesla Now, Bloomberg comes with fresh details about these plans, which appear to have advanced significantly. As I wrote in October, Tesla annual shareholder meeting on December 3 looks like the perfect opportunity to announce the merger plans to shareholders. This should allow Tesla to hold a vote on the merger in early 2027.
According to Bloomberg, Tesla and SpaceX teams have been drawing up the terms of the tie-up and the governance structure of the combined entity, among other matters. If successful, the merger would be the biggest-ever merger deal, potentially creating a $3.5 trillion company. That would put it in the top 5 most valuable companies, ahead of Amazon and in spitting distance of Google.
However, it's not going to be easy to sell this deal to Tesla shareholders, and it's likely that SpaceX will have to pay a premium to convince them. Even if the deal is successful, the resulting entity will have to reconcile national security sensitivities around SpaceX's US defense contracts and Tesla's profitable China manufacturing operations. Musk has dismissed rumors about a spin-off of Tesla's Chinese operations, but this might be inevitable.
